newsitem.title: USA: Coca-cola chief richest Hispanic in United States.
newsitem.headline: Coca-cola chief richest Hispanic in United States.

text.p: Roberto Goizueta, chairman and chief executive of Coca-Cola, is the United States' wealthiest Hispanic with a fortune of $846 million, Hispanic Business magazine said in its annual "rich list".

"Thanks to the soaring price of Coca-Cola stock, CEO Roberto Goizueta's value grew $272 million -- at times last year his net worth surpassed the $1 billion mark," the magazine said in its March issue, calling him the first Hispanic to flirt with billionaire status.
He was followed by Joseph Unanue and family of Secaucus, New Jersey, owners of Goya Foods. His net worth was put at $475 million.
Cuban Americans such as the Havana-born Goizueta dominated the list of 80 people, with those of Mexican origin next. Twenty three people lived in Miami, followed by 14 living in California.

Well-known names included Latin pop superstar Gloria Estefan and her husband Emilio, whose net worth was listed as $100 million. They were in 12th place, their treasure boosted last year by real estate holdings, record sales and a major concert tour.
Businessman and Cuban American political leader Jorge Mas Canosa, who harbours ambitions of one day replacing Cuban President Fidel Castro, was placed fifth with a net worth of $257 million.
His 34-year-old son, also named Jorge, pipped him to fourth place with a $329 million fortune.
MasTec Inc, controlled by the Canosas, more than doubled their reveue by acquiring Spanish telecommunications company Sintel and U.S. contractor Harrison-Wright.
And what do they do with all that money?
"Mr. Mas Canosa hopes to gain leverage in influencing Spain's policy towards Cuba," Hispanic Business said.
On the other hand Gedalio Grimberg, chairman of watchmaker Movada and tagged at $66 million, spent $62,000 on a Piaget watch from Jacqueline Onassis' estate.
A person or family had to be worth at least $25 million to make the list and the combined net worth of the 80 was $7.04 billion.
The magazine asked what motivated millionaires to keep working even after their coffers were overflowing.
"I don't believe in retirement," said 61-year-old Amancio Suarze, who among other things has a 10 per cent interest in the Miami Heat basketball team.
"Also, I have my family coming along after me and they will enjoy what I pass on to them."
The magazine's advice to aspiring multi-millionaires: "Stick do what you well. Successful wealth-builders tend to stick to their area of expertise, whether it's investment banking or pop music.
"Over the years their style -- aggressive, elegant or calculating -- doesn't change much either."
